subject: caterpillar bodyguard
title: A Wasp Turns a Caterpillar Into a Bodyguard for Its Own Killers

scenes.text: This caterpillar is guarding the babies that ate it alive.
A tiny wasp stabbed up to 80 eggs into it. The larvae grew inside, feeding on its body.
Then they burst out through its skin and spun cocoons beside it. The caterpillar didn't die.
It stopped eating. It stopped moving. It stood over the cocoons and head-butted anything that came close.
One or two larvae stay behind inside, still steering it. Guarded cocoons lost half as many to predators.
The wasps hatched. Then the bodyguard dropped dead. Job done.

description:
A Glyptapanteles wasp lays up to 80 eggs in a caterpillar; the larvae eat it from inside, burst out and spin cocoons, and the caterpillar then stands guard over them, head-butting predators away.
In the 2008 PLoS ONE study, guarded cocoons suffered half the predation of unguarded ones, and one or two larvae stayed inside the host, apparently controlling it. The caterpillar never eats again and dies when the adult wasps emerge.
Is this the cruelest trick in nature? Comment below.
first_comment: The wasp is Glyptapanteles, a few millimetres long. Only 1 in 20 healthy caterpillars ever head-butts a predator; nearly every infected one does. Which parasite should we cover next?
